claims.text: Adding approximately 1–2 vol% Y2O3 nanoparticles by mechanical alloying will improve the radiation tolerance of a refractory high-entropy alloy.
A low-volume-fraction Y2O3 dispersion will preserve the alloy's mechanical integrity under plasma-facing irradiation conditions.
The proposed oxide-dispersion intervention is practical for engineering-scale plasma-facing applications.
Mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering will produce a homogeneous dispersion of Y2O3 nanoparticles throughout the RHEA matrix.
Ion irradiation at approximately 500°C in inert or vacuum conditions can simulate relevant aspects of neutron-induced damage under plasma-facing conditions.
Uniformly dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles are stable defect sinks in the refractory high-entropy-alloy matrix.
Y2O3 nanoparticles act as barriers to dislocation movement.
The oxide dispersoids capture radiation-induced vacancies and interstitials and promote their recombination.
Enhanced vacancy-interstitial recombination reduces irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Reduced defect accumulation lowers radiation-induced swelling and embrittlement without a significant loss of mechanical performance.
After identical irradiation, the Y2O3-modified alloy will have a lower irradiation-induced defect density than the unmodified alloy.
After identical irradiation, the Y2O3-modified alloy will exhibit less swelling than the unmodified alloy.
After identical irradiation, the Y2O3-modified alloy will retain higher hardness than the unmodified alloy.
After identical irradiation, the Y2O3-modified alloy will retain higher tensile strength than the unmodified alloy.
The beneficial effect requires a homogeneous oxide dispersion and an oxide content near 1–2 vol%.
Excessive oxide additions or inhomogeneous dispersions may cause embrittlement or degradation of engineering properties.
